templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Insects resting motionless on foliage are acoustically camouflaged from echolocating bats, since a leaf returns a strong echo that obscures the comparatively faint echo of an insect on it. Using a biomimetic sonar device, Inga Geipel and colleagues measured echoes from leaves, with and without insects, from more than 500 angles. Sound striking a leaf nearly head-on produced a strong echo regardless of whether an insect was present, whereas sound arriving at a steep angle was largely deflected elsewhere, much as light is reflected by a mirror. Common big-eared bats hunting in a flight cage approached prey-bearing leaves at such steep angles almost 80 percent of the time.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the bats’ steep angles of approach?
options: They likely make an insect’s echo stronger than it would be in a head-on approach, since a leaf struck at a steep angle directs sound toward any insect resting on it.
They likely keep insects from noticing the bats’ calls, since most of the sound that strikes a leaf at such an angle is deflected away from the insect on it.
They likely allow the bats to pick out an insect’s echo, since the leaf beneath the insect then sends little of its own echo back toward the bats.
They likely let the bats locate prey-bearing leaves from farther away, since a leaf deflects sound arriving at a steep angle much as a mirror reflects light.
items.explanation: The text says that a leaf’s strong echo masks the faint echo of an insect on it, that a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects most of the sound away instead of sending it back, and that the bats approached leaves with prey at such angles almost 80 percent of the time. Together these points suggest that the steep approach lets the bats hear the insect’s echo because the leaf’s own echo no longer drowns it out.

A.why_wrong: The text says a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects sound away; it never says the leaf directs sound toward the insect or makes the insect’s echo stronger. What changes is that the leaf’s masking echo is removed.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether insects can hear the bats, and it says sound is deflected away from the bat’s side of the leaf, not away from the insect.

D.recipe: true detail with an unsupported conclusion
D.why_wrong: The deflection is real, but it sends the sound elsewhere instead of back to the bats, so it would not help them find leaves from a distance. What the steep approach does is remove the leaf’s masking echo so that the insect’s echo stands out.

sources.what: Geipel, Steckel, Tschapka et al., Current Biology 2019: leaves mask echoes of silent prey; biomimetic sonar from many angles; leaves act as specular reflectors at oblique angles; wild bats (Micronycteris microtis, common big-eared bat) in a flight cage approached prey from the predicted oblique angles (press accounts: over 500 angles, nearly 80 percent of approaches in the reflecting range)

items.notes: Natural science (sensory ecology). P1: a leaf’s echo masks the insect’s, and a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects sound away; P2: bats approach prey-bearing leaves at those angles; unstated conclusion: the approach removes the masking echo so the insect’s echo stands out. Press figures: 500+ angles, 42 to 78 degrees optimal, almost 80 percent of approaches.

fixes: hardened to band 6: D (head-on approaches confirm prey) fell to the stated head-on fact; now it keeps the true mirror-like deflection and draws an unsupported conclusion (finding leaves from farther away), which fails only once the student sees the deflected sound does not come back; re-solved blind, C only

items.passage: Genetic analyses indicate that the human populations of eastern and southern Africa became separated sometime between about 350,000 and 70,000 years ago. Comparing ostrich eggshell beads excavated at sites across both regions, archaeologists Jennifer Miller and Yiming Wang determined that beads made in southern Africa between about 50,000 and 33,000 years ago closely resembled, in their dimensions and central perforations, those produced some 3,000 kilometers away in eastern Africa. After about 33,000 years ago, the two regions’ bead styles diverged, a change the researchers associate with a climatic shift that brought periodic flooding to the Zambezi River basin, which lies between them.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about the populations of eastern and southern Africa?
options: They likely remained in contact with each other until a later time than the genetic evidence alone would indicate.
They likely developed their bead-making methods independently, producing similar beads because both relied on ostrich eggshell as a material.
They likely formed a single population until about 33,000 years ago, when flooding in the Zambezi River basin divided them.
They likely began making ostrich eggshell beads in southern Africa before the practice was adopted in eastern Africa.
items.explanation: The bead styles of the two regions matched until about 33,000 years ago and then diverged when flooding disrupted the basin between them, which indicates that the similarity depended on contact across that area. Because the genetic studies place the populations’ divergence between 350,000 and 70,000 years ago, the beads suggest the populations stayed connected well after the genetic evidence alone would indicate.

B.why_wrong: If the two regions had developed similar beads independently, flooding between them would not explain why their styles diverged; the researchers’ link between the flooding and the divergence points to contact, not independent invention.

C.why_wrong: Genetic analyses place the separation of the two populations between about 350,000 and 70,000 years ago. The matching beads point to continued contact between separate populations, not to their being one population until 33,000 years ago.

D.why_wrong: The text never says where ostrich eggshell beads were first made; it only compares beads from the two regions over the same period.

sources.what: Miller and Wang, Nature 2022 (Ostrich eggshell beads reveal 50,000-year-old social network in Africa), abstract: genetic divergence of eastern and southern African lineages about 350 to 70 ka; bead connection about 50 to 33 ka over about 3,000 km; breakdown about 33 ka matching southward ITCZ shift and periodic flooding of the Zambezi catchment; implies a later regional divergence than genetic analyses predict

items.notes: Archaeology. P1: genetic divergence dated 350,000 to 70,000 years ago; P2: bead styles matched until about 33,000 years ago and diverged when flooding cut the connecting basin (so similarity reflects contact); unstated conclusion: contact lasted later than the genetic dates imply (the paper’s own conclusion, left unstated in the passage).

fixes: hardened to band 6: C (stopped making beads) fell to the word diverged; now an overreach that reads the bead contact as one undivided population until 33,000 years ago, killed only by linking it to the genetic separation dates; re-solved blind, A only

items.passage: Engineers Chelsea Heveran, Wil Srubar, and colleagues have developed a building material that is partly alive. They mixed sand and a gelatin-based hydrogel with Synechococcus, a photosynthetic bacterium that toughens the mixture by depositing calcium carbonate, the mineral found in seashells. Because the bacteria live on inside the material, a single block supplied with fresh sand, hydrogel, and nutrients under warm, humid conditions could seed new blocks through three successive generations. The researchers found, however, that the material was strongest when thoroughly dried, and that prolonged dryness sharply reduced the share of its bacteria that survived.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about a block of the material that has been kept in very dry conditions for a long time?
options: It would likely be stronger than a block kept moist and just as able to seed new blocks, since its bacteria would already have deposited their calcium carbonate.
It would likely regain its full population of living bacteria as soon as it was returned to warm and humid conditions.
It would likely contain less calcium carbonate than the blocks it was used to seed, since each new block draws its minerals from the one before it.
It would likely make a sturdier building component than a block kept moist, but a poorer source of new blocks.
items.explanation: The text says the material is strongest when thoroughly dried, so a block kept dry would be sturdy. It also says that new blocks can be seeded only because the bacteria live on inside the material, and that prolonged dryness sharply reduces how many bacteria survive. A long-dried block would therefore have fewer living bacteria to seed new blocks.

A.why_wrong: The block would likely be stronger, but prolonged dryness kills many of its bacteria, and seeding new blocks depends on living bacteria, so it would not be just as able to seed new ones.

B.why_wrong: The text says regeneration took place under warm, humid conditions with living bacteria, but it never says bacteria killed by dryness recover once moisture returns.

C.recipe: invented comparison with a wrong mechanism
C.why_wrong: The text never compares the calcium carbonate in parent and offspring blocks, and it says new blocks were supplied with fresh sand, hydrogel, and nutrients rather than drawing minerals from the parent.

sources.what: Heveran, Williams, Qiu, Artier, Hubler, Cook, Cameron and Srubar, Matter 2020 (Biomineralization and Successive Regeneration of Engineered Living Building Materials), abstract: sand-hydrogel scaffold inoculated with Synechococcus sp. PCC 7002, toughened by calcium carbonate biomineralization; three successive regenerations from one parent using temperature and humidity switches; structural function maximized at ultradesiccated conditions while prolonged dehydration compromised microbial viability

items.notes: Technology (materials). P1: dry material is strongest; P2: regeneration depends on living bacteria, and prolonged dryness kills them; unstated conclusion: a long-dried block trades regenerative ability for strength. Hydrogel was gelatin-based (press coverage); detail not used by the item.

items.passage: Arguments that games constitute an art form have frequently centered on the narratives games tell or the fictional worlds they depict, effectively treating games as a kind of interactive cinema. Philosopher C. Thi Nguyen locates their artistry elsewhere. A game designer, he observes, determines not only the world of a game but also who the player will be within it, specifying which abilities the player may use, which obstacles stand in the way, and which objectives the player is to pursue. In Nguyen’s view, then, what distinguishes games from the other arts is that their medium is agency itself.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Nguyen argues that games, like films, are art chiefly because of the worlds they depict, though designers also decide which abilities players have within those worlds.
Nguyen contends that games are distinctive among the arts because their designers shape the very capacities and aims with which players act, not just the settings of play.
Although games, like films, often tell stories, Nguyen maintains that the obstacles games present make them more demanding of their audiences than other art forms are.
Nguyen holds that because designers dictate players’ goals and abilities, games restrict players’ freedom in ways that keep games from fully qualifying as art.
items.explanation: The text says that Nguyen looks beyond stories and worlds, arguing that a designer also determines who the player will be: the abilities, obstacles, and goals the player works with. His conclusion is that games stand apart from the other arts because their medium is agency, which is what choice B states.

A.why_wrong: Designers do decide players’ abilities, but Nguyen locates the artistry of games elsewhere than in the worlds they depict; for him, shaping who the player is within the game is the art, not an addition to it.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions obstacles as one thing designers specify, but it never says games are more demanding of their audiences than other art forms.

D.why_wrong: Nguyen treats the designer’s control over goals and abilities as what makes games a distinctive art form, not as something that keeps them from qualifying as art.

sources.what: C. Thi Nguyen, Games: Agency as Art (Oxford University Press, 2020), book abstract: games are a unique art form; designers do not just create a world but who you will be in it, telling you what abilities to use and what goals to take on; games work in the medium of agency

items.notes: Humanities (philosophy of art). Scholar-argument passage like 3.20: a common framing, then the scholar’s alternative, then its conclusion. The opening framing is kept generic (no named holder).

fixes: hardened to band 6: A was the rejected worlds view plus an invented comparison; now a half-true compound (true clause on designers deciding abilities, wrong locus of artistry); re-solved blind, B only

items.passage: Literary scholars have traditionally built their claims on the careful reading of individual works. But as literary historian Franco Moretti observed in 2000, even a specialist in nineteenth-century European fiction really knows only its canonical fraction, which amounts to less than one percent of the novels published; tens of thousands of British novels from that century alone have gone unread, and no one will ever read them all. Since reading more cannot close a gap of that size, Moretti argued, studying literature on a world scale requires a fundamentally different critical method.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although literary study has long relied on close attention to particular texts, Moretti argued that the vast quantity of unread works demands a different way of studying literature.
Moretti argued that scholars of nineteenth-century fiction should replace the canonical novels they study with lesser-known ones, since the canon represents only a tiny share of what was published.
Moretti contended that nineteenth-century British novels have received far more scholarly attention than novels written in other parts of the world during the same period.
Moretti argued that because the canon is only a tiny share of what was published, the careful reading of individual works no longer has any value for literary scholars.
items.explanation: The text sets the traditional practice of careful reading against Moretti’s observation that the canon is under one percent of published novels and that most novels will never be read. Because reading more cannot close that gap, he argued that a different method is needed, which choice A captures along with the practice it departs from.

B.why_wrong: Moretti argues that reading more cannot solve the problem, so swapping canonical novels for other novels to read would not meet his call for a different method; the text never proposes such a swap.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions British novels only as an example of how many works go unread; it never compares the attention they receive with that given to novels from elsewhere.

D.why_wrong: Moretti says that reading more cannot close the gap and that studying literature on a world scale needs a different method; the text never says that careful reading of individual works has no value.

sources.what: Franco Moretti, Conjectures on World Literature, New Left Review 1 (January to February 2000): he works on the canonical fraction, not even one per cent of published literature; thirty to sixty thousand nineteenth-century British novels no one has read or ever will; reading more is not the solution; world literature asks for a new critical method

items.notes: Humanities (literary history). Two-part main idea with a concession, like 3.21 and 3.16. Moretti’s method (distant reading) left unnamed so the key stays a paraphrase.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage wording (close attention to particular texts, a different way of studying literature)
hardened to band 6: D (restrict claims to the canon) was a flat contradiction; now an overstatement that keeps the canon fact and claims careful reading has no value; re-solved blind, A only

items.passage: Through most of the twentieth century, many researchers regarded Amazonia as a largely untouched wilderness, assuming that its early inhabitants had done little to transform the landscape. Work by Umberto Lombardo and colleagues in the Llanos de Moxos, a seasonally flooded savanna in Bolivia, tells a different story. The roughly 4,700 forested islands that dot this otherwise treeless plain turn out to be human-made, the earliest begun about 10,850 years ago, and plant remains preserved in their soils show that squash and manioc were being cultivated there by about 10,250 years ago.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Lombardo and colleagues found that early inhabitants of the Llanos de Moxos cleared much of the forest that once covered the region so that they could grow squash and manioc.
Researchers have concluded that farming in Amazonia began in the Llanos de Moxos and spread from there to other parts of the region over thousands of years.
Because the Llanos de Moxos floods every year, its early inhabitants built forested islands mainly as places to escape rising water rather than as places to farm.
Although Amazonia was long thought to have been little changed by its early inhabitants, evidence from Bolivia shows people reshaping the land and growing crops there over 10,000 years ago.
items.explanation: The text first gives the long-held view that early inhabitants did little to reshape Amazonia, then says Lombardo’s work tells a different story: people built thousands of forested islands starting about 10,850 years ago and grew squash and manioc there by about 10,250 years ago. Choice D states both the earlier view and the evidence that revises it.

A.recipe: twisted detail (creating forest read as clearing it)
A.why_wrong: The text says the forested islands on the plain are human-made, so people created patches of forest rather than clearing one, and it never says the plain was once covered by forest.

B.why_wrong: The text shows early cultivation in the Llanos de Moxos but never says farming in Amazonia began there or spread from there.

C.why_wrong: The text never says why the islands were built, and it says plant remains in their soils show crops were cultivated there, so they were not mainly refuges from water rather than farmland.

sources.what: Lombardo, Iriarte, Hilbert et al., Nature 2020 (Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia), abstract: squash about 10,250 and manioc about 10,350 cal yr BP in the Llanos de Moxos, Bolivia; starting about 10,850 cal yr BP people created about 4,700 artificial forest islands in a treeless, seasonally flooded savannah; humans have altered the Amazonian landscape since their arrival

items.notes: Archaeology (view then correction). The earlier view is the familiar pristine-wilderness picture of Amazonia, kept unattributed. Dates: squash about 10,250 and manioc about 10,350 cal yr BP, so both were cultivated by about 10,250 years ago.

fixes: hardened to band 6: A (islands formed naturally) fell to the stated human-made fact; now keeps the true early cultivation of squash and manioc but turns created forest into cleared forest; re-solved blind, D only

items.passage:
The following text is from Ivor Gurney’s 1917 poem “The Fire Kindled.” Gurney wrote the poem while serving as an infantryman during World War I. Dymock and Malvern are localities near his childhood home in Gloucestershire, in western England.

The star of afterglow,
Venus, on western hills;
Dymock in spring: O spring
Of home! O daffodils!

And Malvern’s matchless huge
Bastions of ancient fires—
These will not let me rest,
So hot my heart desires....

Here we go sore of shoulder,
Sore of foot, by quiet streams;
But these are not my rivers....
And these are useless dreams.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker celebrates the landscapes of his home as worth the hardships he now endures as a soldier.
The speaker longs for the familiar places of his home, though he recognizes that such longing does him no good where he is.
The speaker contrasts the beauty of his home with the place where he now marches and resolves to put thoughts of home aside.
The speaker looks forward to the spring, when he expects to return home and see the daffodils of Dymock again.
items.explanation: The speaker calls up places near his home, Dymock in spring and Malvern’s hills, and says they “will not let me rest, / So hot my heart desires.” In the last stanza he notes that the streams where he marches “are not my rivers” and that his thoughts of home “are useless dreams.” He longs for home while seeing that the longing cannot help him.

A.why_wrong: The speaker does praise the places of home, but he says they “will not let me rest” and calls his thoughts of them “useless dreams”; he never presents them as making the hardships of marching worthwhile.

C.why_wrong: The speaker does set home against the place where he marches, but the places of home “will not let me rest”; he never resolves to stop thinking of them.

D.why_wrong: Dymock in spring is something the speaker longs for, not a return he expects; he calls such thoughts “useless dreams.”

sources.what: Ivor Gurney, Severn & Somme (London: Sidgwick & Jackson, 1917), poem The Fire Kindled, last three stanzas copied exactly (Project Gutenberg 63895); the preface says the book was written while he served with the Gloucesters

items.notes: Literary (poem). Excerpt is the last three of six stanzas, copied exactly (four-dot ellipses as printed). Gurney is not in any official item or ours (grep). Places glossed in the context sentence, as 3.17 glosses its terms.

fixes: hardened to band 6: A (quiet streams comfort him) fell to the quoted line these are not my rivers; now a plausible imported reading (home landscapes justify the soldier’s hardships), true on praise of home and unsupported on the rest; re-solved blind, B only

items.passage: Asian honeybees (Apis cerana) in Vietnam are preyed upon by the giant hornet Vespa soror, which attacks colonies collectively, landing at a hive’s entrance and chewing through it to reach the developing brood inside. Heather Mattila and colleagues documented a remarkable countermeasure: following such attacks, worker bees gathered fragments of animal dung and applied spots of it around their hives’ entrances. The bees did not respond this way to a smaller hornet species that rarely lands at entrances. Heavily spotted entrances experienced fewer coordinated attacks, and hornets arriving at them were substantially less likely to land and chew.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one effect of heavy dung spotting around a hive’s entrance?
options: It draws the smaller hornet species away from the hive and toward colonies that have not been spotted.
It leads Vespa soror hornets to attack the hive in groups rather than one at a time.
It allows worker bees to tell which hives have already been attacked by hornets.
It makes Vespa soror hornets less likely to land on the entrance and chew through it.
items.explanation: The last sentence of the text says that heavily spotted entrances experienced fewer coordinated attacks and that hornets arriving at them were much less likely to land and chew. So one effect of the spotting is that Vespa soror hornets are less likely to land on the entrance and chew through it.

A.why_wrong: The text says the bees do not spot their entrances in response to the smaller hornet; it never says spotting draws that hornet toward other colonies.

B.why_wrong: Heavily spotted entrances experienced fewer coordinated attacks, not more.

C.why_wrong: The text never says the spots help bees identify which hives have been attacked; it describes their effect on the hornets.

sources.what: Mattila, Otis, Nguyen, Pham, Knight and Phan, PLOS ONE 2020 (Honey bees (Apis cerana) use animal feces as a tool to defend colonies against group attack by giant hornets (Vespa soror)), abstract: workers foraged for and applied spots of animal feces around nest entrances after V. soror attacks; no spotting in response to V. velutina, a smaller hornet that rarely lands at entrances; moderate to heavy spotting lowered multiple-hornet attacks and substantially reduced the likelihood of hornets approaching and chewing on entrances

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Explicit detail: the key paraphrases the last sentence; B reverses it, A recombines the smaller-hornet detail.

items.passage: Filipino composer Lucrecia Kasilag (1918–2008) trained as a pianist and later studied composition at the Eastman School of Music in New York. After completing her studies, she toured internationally as a concert pianist, but a congenital weakness in one hand eventually forced her to abandon performing. She also served as dean of a college of music and fine arts in Manila and later as president of the Cultural Center of the Philippines. Devoting herself chiefly to composition, she produced more than 350 works and became particularly celebrated for incorporating indigenous Filipino instruments into orchestral music.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Kasilag stop performing as a concert pianist?
options: She wished to write music for indigenous Filipino instruments.
A physical condition affecting one of her hands made it impossible to continue.
She was appointed to lead a college of music and fine arts in Manila.
She came to prefer Filipino music to Western concert works.
items.explanation: The text says that Kasilag toured as a concert pianist but that a congenital weakness in one hand eventually forced her to abandon performing. That weakness is the physical condition described in choice B.

A.why_wrong: The text says she devoted herself to composition after she had to stop performing; it does not say a wish to compose made her stop.

C.why_wrong: The text says she served as a dean in Manila, but it does not give that as the reason she stopped performing.

D.why_wrong: The text never says she came to prefer Filipino music to Western works; it says she brought Filipino instruments into orchestral music.

sources.what: Lucrecia Kasilag (1918 to 2008), National Artist for Music: studied at the Eastman School of Music; after her studies made an international tour as a concert pianist but had to give up a performing career due to a congenital weakness in one hand; dean of the Philippine Women’s University College of Music and Fine Arts from 1953; more than 350 compositions; known for incorporating indigenous Filipino instruments into orchestral productions

items.notes: Arts (music). Explicit detail, one reason stem like 2.10; C is a true detail that does not answer the question.

items.passage: Rock paintings throughout the Sahara depict herders tending cattle, and a few appear to show cows being milked, but such images can rarely be dated reliably. Because cattle bones are scarce at Saharan archaeological sites, researchers also cannot determine from the animals’ ages at slaughter whether herders kept them primarily for milk. Julie Dunne and colleagues therefore analyzed fatty residues absorbed into ancient pottery from Takarkori, a rock shelter in southwestern Libya, and identified the distinctive chemical signature of milk fat in vessels produced roughly 7,000 years ago.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Rock paintings in the Sahara show that herders there began milking cattle at about the same time that they began making pottery.
Dunne and colleagues determined from cattle bones at Takarkori the ages at which early Saharan herders typically slaughtered their animals.
Chemical analysis of pottery has provided evidence of milk use in the ancient Sahara that other kinds of evidence could not reliably supply.
Researchers have been able to date the Saharan rock paintings that show milking scenes by studying the residues in pottery found near the paintings.
items.explanation: The text explains that rock paintings cannot be dated reliably and that too few cattle bones survive to show whether herders kept cattle for milk. It then says Dunne and colleagues found the chemical signature of milk fat in pottery about 7,000 years old, evidence that the other sources could not provide.

A.why_wrong: The text says the paintings can rarely be dated reliably and never links the start of milking to the start of pottery making.

B.why_wrong: The text says cattle bones are too scarce to show slaughter ages, which is why the researchers turned to pottery.

D.why_wrong: The pottery residues dated milk use itself; the text never says they were used to date the paintings.

sources.what: Dunne, Evershed, Salque et al., Nature 2012 (First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium BC), abstract: rock art depicts cattle herding and rare milking scenes but can rarely be reliably dated; scarcity of cattle bones precludes kill-off analysis; first unequivocal chemical evidence (delta 13C and Delta 13C of milk fat alkanoic acids in pottery) of dairying in the fifth millennium BC; pottery from Takarkori rock shelter, Libyan Acacus

items.notes: Archaeology. Main idea spread across the passage: two failed lines of evidence, then the new method and finding; key abstracts the finding to milk use and keeps the contrast. Fifth millennium BC given as roughly 7,000 years ago.

items.passage: In experiments by Sylvain Alem, Lars Chittka, and colleagues, bumblebees were offered artificial flowers containing sugar water that sat beneath a transparent table, out of reach unless the bees pulled on attached strings. Only a few bees discovered the solution independently, but most could be trained through a series of incremental steps, and untrained bees acquired the technique simply by observing a trained one. When a single knowledgeable bee was introduced into a colony, string pulling spread to most of the colony’s foragers, with newly skilled bees in turn serving as demonstrators for others.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research suggests that bumblebees can learn an unfamiliar skill by watching other bees, allowing the skill to spread through a colony.
Researchers found that most bumblebees can work out on their own how to obtain food that has been placed out of their reach.
Bumblebees in the experiments could learn string pulling only by watching another bee perform the technique in front of them.
Experiments showed that bumblebees learn string pulling far more readily when they are kept in a colony than when they are tested on their own.
items.explanation: The text describes how untrained bees learned string pulling by watching a trained bee and how the technique then spread from one knowledgeable bee to most of a colony’s foragers. Choice A states this finding: bees can pick up an unfamiliar skill by observation, which lets it spread.

B.why_wrong: Only a few bees discovered the solution on their own; most had to be trained or had to watch another bee.

C.why_wrong: Observation was one way to learn, but the text says most bees could also be trained through incremental steps.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how readily bees learn in a colony with how readily they learn when tested alone.

sources.what: Alem, Perry, Zhu, Loukola, Ingraham, Sovik and Chittka, PLOS Biology 2016 (Associative Mechanisms Allow for Social Learning and Cultural Transmission of String Pulling in an Insect), abstract: only a small minority solved the task spontaneously; most learned with stepwise training; naive bees learned by observing a trained demonstrator; in diffusion experiments the skill spread from a single knowledgeable individual to most of a colony’s foragers, with observers becoming demonstrators for later learners

items.notes: Natural science (animal cognition). Study report; key abstracts the finding (social learning that spreads) rather than the task. Flowers sat under a transparent Plexiglas table in the study.

items.passage: English speakers tend to describe durations in terms of distance, speaking of a “long” meeting, whereas Greek speakers more often describe them in terms of quantity, speaking of “much” time. To test whether such linguistic habits influence nonlinguistic thinking, Daniel Casasanto and colleagues showed participants animations of lines extending across a screen and of containers gradually filling, then asked them to estimate how long each animation had lasted. English speakers’ estimates were swayed more by how far a line extended, while Greek speakers’ estimates were swayed more by how full a container became.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Greek speakers estimated how long the animations lasted more accurately than English speakers did, regardless of what the animations showed.
Casasanto and colleagues found that both groups judged growing lines to last longer than filling containers.
An experiment suggests that the way a language usually describes time may affect how its speakers judge durations, even when no words are involved.
Although Greek and English speakers describe time in the same way, they differ in how they perceive distance and quantity in animations.
items.explanation: The text says English speakers talk about time as distance and Greek speakers as quantity, and that in a task with no words, English speakers’ time estimates were swayed more by distance and Greek speakers’ by fullness. The experiment therefore suggests that a language’s usual way of describing time may shape how its speakers judge durations.

A.why_wrong: The text reports which cues swayed each group’s estimates, not which group estimated more accurately.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares how long lines and containers seemed to last; it compares which kind of animation swayed each group more.

D.why_wrong: The text says the two groups describe time differently, as distance and as quantity, and links the difference in estimates to that difference.

sources.what: Casasanto, Fotakopoulou, Lucero, Pita and Boroditsky, Language and Cognition 18 (2026), The long and small of it: Language shapes duration estimation in speakers of English and Greek: English speakers describe duration mainly as length (a long night), Greek speakers as amount (poli ora, much time); in nonlinguistic tasks lines grew across the screen and containers filled; English speakers’ estimates were swayed more by irrelevant length, Greek speakers’ by irrelevant amount (fullness)

items.notes: Social science (linguistics and cognition). Study report with the governing claim left for the student to state; key carries the hedge (suggests, may).

fixes: source replaced: the 2008 Language Learning abstract did not state the English and Greek details; Casasanto et al., Language and Cognition 2026 states the length and amount metaphors, the growing-line and filling-container tasks and the matching effects; passage unchanged

items.passage: Swedish Sámi artist Britta Marakatt-Labba, who grew up in a reindeer-herding family, is internationally recognized for narrative embroideries that draw on Sámi culture and mythology. In The Crows, created in response to the Alta conflict, a controversy in the late 1970s over plans to dam a river in northern Norway, crows landing near Sámi demonstrators transform into black-clad police officers as they march uphill. Her Historjá (2003–2007), an embroidered work more than 23 meters long, chronicles the history and mythology of the Sámi people.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Marakatt-Labba’s embroideries mainly record her own family’s experiences of herding reindeer in northern Sweden.
Marakatt-Labba uses embroidery to tell stories of Sámi life, history, and belief, including events of her own lifetime.
Marakatt-Labba turned from embroidery to other art forms after creating a work about the Alta conflict.
Historjá is widely considered Marakatt-Labba’s most celebrated work because of its unusual length and its ambitious subject matter.
items.explanation: The text says Marakatt-Labba is known for narrative embroideries drawn from Sámi culture and mythology and gives two examples: The Crows, about a recent Sámi protest, and Historjá, which recounts Sámi history and mythology. Choice B generalizes from these examples.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that she grew up in a reindeer-herding family, but her works as described are about Sámi culture, protest, history, and mythology, not mainly her family.

C.why_wrong: The text describes Historjá, an embroidery made decades after The Crows, so she did not turn away from embroidery.

D.why_wrong: The text gives Historjá’s length but never says it is her most celebrated work.

sources.what: Britta Marakatt-Labba (born 1951), Sámi textile artist from a reindeer-herding family, known for narrative embroidery using motifs from Sámi culture and mythology; The Crows (Garjját), made in connection with the Alta conflict, shows crows near Sámi protesters turning into black-clad police officers marching up the hill; Historjá (2003 to 2007), 23.5 m long, tells the history and mythology of the Sámi people, shown at documenta 14 (2017)

items.notes: Arts (textile art). Profile with two examples; key generalizes, as in 2.9. The Alta conflict glossed in place.

items.passage:
The following text is from Katharine Tynan’s 1909 novel Mary Gray. Mary, a girl from an impoverished household on Wistaria Terrace, now lives with Lady Anne, a wealthy elderly woman, as her companion.

Once again she longed for Wistaria Terrace. There was no place for her in this world, she said to herself; and sent a tender reproach in her own mind to the father who had given her up for her good. Then she felt contrite about Lady Anne. How good the old lady was to her, and how she stood up for her, would stand up for her, even to the terrible Lady Drummond! Still, it was not her world; it never would be. She thought, with sudden childish tears filling her eyes, that the next time Lady Anne went to see any of her fine friends she would pray to be left at home.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Mary resents Lady Anne for having taken her away from her family and her home on Wistaria Terrace.
Mary decides to return to Wistaria Terrace because Lady Drummond has made her feel unwelcome.
Mary is confident that Lady Anne will always defend her, so she no longer worries about what Lady Anne’s fine friends might think of her.
Although Mary is grateful for Lady Anne’s kindness, she feels that she will never belong in Lady Anne’s world.
items.explanation: Mary longs for Wistaria Terrace and tells herself there is no place for her in this world. She feels contrite when she remembers how good Lady Anne is to her, yet she thinks “it was not her world; it never would be.” Choice D captures both her gratitude and her sense of not belonging.

A.why_wrong: Mary’s “tender reproach” is aimed at her father, and she feels contrite about Lady Anne, so she does not resent Lady Anne.

B.why_wrong: Mary longs for home and hopes to be left at home on future visits, but she never decides to go back to Wistaria Terrace.

C.why_wrong: Mary does believe Lady Anne will stand up for her, but she still feels out of place and is near tears, so she is far from untroubled.

sources.what: Katharine Tynan, Mary Gray (1909), chapter 4 (Boy and Girl), paragraph copied exactly from Project Gutenberg 20201 (italic this printed plain)

items.notes: Literary prose. Two-part key with a concession, as in 1.14. Tynan is not in any official item or ours (grep). Mary has just overheard Lady Drummond speak unkindly of her; the context line leaves that out since the excerpt names her.

items.passage: In the weeks after a devastating earthquake shook Edo (present-day Tokyo) in 1855, great numbers of woodblock prints called namazu-e, or catfish pictures, circulated through the city. According to popular belief, earthquakes were caused by a gigantic catfish thrashing beneath the earth, and many prints depict a protective deity pinning the creature down with a stone. Others portray the catfish more generously. Reconstruction required enormous expenditures, a large share of them disbursed by wealthy households, and in some prints construction workers celebrate the catfish as gold coins shower down around them.
items.stem: Based on the text, why do some namazu-e most likely show construction workers celebrating the catfish?
options: The workers believed that the deity had finally pinned the catfish beneath its stone.
The prints were meant to reassure the public that another earthquake was unlikely to strike Edo soon.
The rebuilding that followed the earthquake gave them work paid for with money from wealthy households.
The workers had predicted the earthquake by watching catfish in nearby rivers.
items.explanation: The text says that rebuilding Edo required vast expenditures, much of them paid out by wealthy households, and that in some prints construction workers celebrate the catfish while gold coins rain down. Putting these together, the prints most likely show the workers celebrating because the earthquake led to rebuilding work that paid them with money from the wealthy.

A.why_wrong: Prints showing the deity pinning the catfish are a different group of prints; the celebrating workers appear in prints that treat the catfish generously.

B.why_wrong: The text never says the prints were meant to reassure anyone about future earthquakes.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that people believed a giant catfish caused earthquakes; it says nothing about predicting earthquakes from the behavior of real catfish.

sources.what: Namazu-e, catfish prints printed in great quantity after the 1855 Ansei Edo earthquake; the god of Kashima restrains the earthquake-causing catfish with a stone; the catfish was also hailed as a world-rectifying god because hoarded wealth was disgorged by the earthquake and much money went into rebuilding, with job opportunities redistributing wealth; prints show gold coins scattered (Gregory Smits, Journal of Social History 2006, is the scholarly source)

items.notes: History and art (Edo popular prints). P1: rebuilding cost vast sums paid out by the wealthy; P2: some prints show construction workers cheering the catfish amid falling gold; unstated conclusion: the quake brought paid work. D echoes a real 1855 anecdote the passage does not include.

items.passage:
The following text is Madison Cawein’s 1902 poem “Proem,” which opens his poetry collection A Voice on the Wind.

Oh, for a soul that fulfills
Music like that of a bird!
Thrilling with rapture the hills,
Heedless if any one heard.

Or, like the flower that blooms
Lone in the midst of the trees,
Filling the woods with perfumes,
Careless if any one sees.

Or, like the wandering wind,
Over the meadows that swings,
Bringing wild sweets to mankind,
Knowing not that which it brings.

Oh, for a way to impart
Beauty, no matter how hard!
Like unto nature, whose art
Never once dreams of reward.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker wishes to give beauty as freely as birds, flowers, and the wind do, without seeking notice or reward.
The speaker regrets that the beauty he has worked hard to create has gone unnoticed and unrewarded.
The speaker argues that the beauty found in nature is greater than any beauty that people could ever hope to create through their art.
The speaker describes a walk through hills, woods, and meadows where he hears birds and smells flowers.
items.explanation: The speaker wishes for a soul like a bird that sings “heedless if any one heard,” a flower that blooms “careless if any one sees,” and wind that brings sweetness without knowing it. The last stanza asks for a way to give beauty “like unto nature, whose art / Never once dreams of reward.” He wants to create beauty without seeking notice or reward.

B.why_wrong: The speaker expresses a wish (“Oh, for a soul”), not regret about his own unnoticed work.

C.why_wrong: The speaker holds nature up as a model to imitate; he never ranks nature’s beauty above the beauty of human art.

D.why_wrong: The birds, flowers, and wind are images of the kind of soul the speaker wants, not things he meets on a walk.

sources.what: Madison Cawein, A Voice on the Wind and Other Poems (Louisville: John P. Morton, 1902), opening poem Proem, copied exactly (printed in capitals; set here in ordinary case) from Project Gutenberg 33940

items.notes: Literary (poem). Whole poem. Cawein is not in any official item or ours (grep).

items.passage: From the early 1700s until the 1860s, the Great Dismal Swamp of Virginia and North Carolina sheltered communities of people who had escaped enslavement, known as maroons. Many inhabited islands of elevated, dry ground deep in the swamp’s interior. Archaeologist Dan Sayers, who began investigating these settlements in 2002, and other researchers have found that the residents depended on whatever the swamp provided, even reusing stone tools left behind by Native Americans. Leaving the swamp to obtain supplies was dangerous, since it could lead to recapture.
items.stem: According to the text, why did the people living in the swamp rely on what they could find there?
options: The swamp’s islands held more resources than the land around the swamp.
Leaving the swamp to get goods put them at risk of being recaptured.
Native Americans living in the swamp taught them how to make stone tools.
The deep water around the islands made it impossible to cross the swamp.
items.explanation: The text says that the residents depended on whatever the swamp provided and that leaving the swamp to obtain supplies was dangerous because it could lead to recapture. That risk is the reason given in choice B.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares the resources of the islands with those of the land around the swamp.

C.why_wrong: The text says the residents reused stone tools left behind by Native Americans, not that Native Americans taught them to make tools.

D.why_wrong: The text says leaving the swamp was dangerous because of recapture, not that crossing the swamp was impossible.

sources.what: Great Dismal Swamp maroons: thousands lived in the swamp between about 1700 and the 1860s, mostly on high, dry islands in the interior; research began in 2002 with Dan Sayers of American University; because leaving the area could lead to recapture, inhabitants used what was readily available in the swamp, even recycling tool remnants left by Native Americans

items.notes: History and archaeology. Explicit detail answered by the last sentence; C recombines the Native American tools detail.

items.passage: Ethiopian artist Afewerk Tekle (1932–2012) studied painting, sculpture, and architecture in London. Upon returning home, he traveled extensively through Ethiopia’s provinces to deepen his knowledge of the country and its culture, which he then reflected in his paintings. His best-known work is Total Liberation of Africa, three monumental stained glass windows he designed in 1958 for Africa Hall, the home of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa in Addis Ababa. Covering about 150 square meters, the windows represent the sorrow of Africa’s past, the struggle of its present, and hope for its future.
items.stem: According to the text, what do the stained glass windows in Africa Hall represent?
options: Places Afewerk visited while traveling through Ethiopia’s provinces
Paintings and sculptures that Afewerk studied in London
Africa’s sorrowful past, its struggling present, and a hopeful future
The founding of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa
items.explanation: The last sentence of the text says that the windows represent the sorrow of Africa’s past, the struggle of its present, and hope for its future, as choice C states.

A.why_wrong: The text says Afewerk reflected what he learned in the provinces in his paintings, not that the windows show places he visited.

B.why_wrong: The text says Afewerk studied painting and sculpture in London, but it never says the windows depict works he studied there.

D.why_wrong: The windows are in the building that houses the commission, but the text never says they show its founding.

sources.what: Afewerk Tekle (1932 to 2012), Ethiopian artist; studied at the Central School of Arts and Crafts and the Slade School in London (painting, sculpture, architecture); travelled the provinces of Ethiopia on his return; in 1958 designed Total Liberation of Africa, stained glass in Africa Hall of the UN Economic Commission for Africa, Addis Ababa; three windows of about 150 square meters representing the sorrow of Africa’s past, the struggle of the present, and hope for the future

items.notes: Arts. Explicit detail with noun-phrase options, as in 1.4.

items.passage: Female loggerhead sea turtles return to nest along the same stretch of coast where they hatched, often after spending years migrating thousands of kilometers across the ocean. To learn how they find it, J. Roger Brothers and Kenneth Lohmann compared nineteen years of nesting records from Florida beaches with gradual shifts in Earth’s magnetic field over the same period. Where the shifts squeezed a particular magnetic signature into a shorter stretch of coast, nests became more crowded; where a signature spread over a longer stretch, nests spread out. The researchers think that young turtles learn the magnetic signature of their home beach and later seek it out.
items.stem: According to the text, what do Brothers and Lohmann think helps female loggerheads find the stretch of coast where they hatched?
options: They recognize the magnetic signature of the beach where they hatched.
They follow other turtles that have nested on the same beach before.
They remember how the coastline near the beach looked when they first swam out to sea.
They are guided by warm currents that flow past their home beach.
items.explanation: The text says the researchers think young turtles learn the magnetic signature of their home beach and later seek it out. Recognizing that signature, as choice A says, is how the turtles find the coast where they hatched.

B.why_wrong: The text never says that turtles follow one another to nesting beaches.

C.why_wrong: The text explains the turtles’ homing by the magnetic field, not by what the coastline looks like.

D.why_wrong: Ocean currents and water temperature are never mentioned in the text.

sources.what: Brothers and Lohmann, Current Biology 2015 (Evidence for Geomagnetic Imprinting and Magnetic Navigation in the Natal Homing of Sea Turtles): 19 years of loggerhead nesting data from the Florida coast; nesting density rose where shifts in the magnetic field moved isolines closer together and fell where they moved apart, consistent with turtles imprinting on the magnetic field of their natal beach

items.notes: Natural science (animal navigation). Isoline convergence rendered as a signature squeezed into a shorter stretch of coast.

items.passage: Psychologists Sebastian Kirschner and Michael Tomasello wanted to determine whether making music together influences how young children treat one another. Pairs of four-year-olds participated in a game. For some pairs, the game involved singing, playing percussion instruments, and moving in time to music. For other pairs, the game involved comparable activities and conversation but no singing or music. Afterward, the researchers arranged a small accident in which one child’s marbles spilled, giving the other child a chance to help. Children who had made music together helped their partners more frequently than children who had played the game without music.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Psychologists found that four-year-olds prefer games with singing and percussion instruments to games that involve conversation.
Children who play games without music are unable to cooperate with the partners they play with.
An experiment showed that young children learn music more quickly when they practice with a partner.
An experiment found that making music together may encourage young children to help one another.
items.explanation: The text describes an experiment in which four-year-olds who sang, played percussion instruments, and moved to music together were later more likely to help their partners than children who played a similar game without music. Choice D states this finding.

A.why_wrong: The text never reports which kind of game the children preferred.

B.why_wrong: Children who played without music helped their partners less often, not never.

C.why_wrong: The study measured helping after the game, not how quickly children learned music.

sources.what: Kirschner and Tomasello, Evolution and Human Behavior 31 (2010), Joint music making promotes prosocial behavior in 4-year-old children (full text, Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology): pairs of 4-year-olds in a musical condition (singing, dancing, playing percussion instruments to a song) or a matched non-musical condition with the same joint activity and spoken language; in the helping test one child’s tube spilled its marbles and the partner could help; children helped one another more after joint music making

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). Study report with the finding in the last sentence, as in 1.11; key hedges with may.

fixes: passage narrowed to the paper (full text found, Max Planck PDF): each child had opportunities to assist the partner with small problems overstated the design (one staged accident per pair, one child able to help); now one child’s marbles spill and the other child can help
drumming changed to playing percussion instruments (wooden frog percussion in the paper), also in option A and the explanation
source replaced with the full paper

items.passage: When a star like the Sun exhausts its fuel, it swells into a red giant, engulfing any planets orbiting close to it, and then contracts into a small, extremely dense star called a white dwarf. Astronomers had previously detected debris from disintegrated planets around white dwarfs, but never an intact planet orbiting close to one. In 2020, Andrew Vanderburg and colleagues reported an object, very likely a planet comparable in size to Jupiter, circling the white dwarf WD 1856+534 approximately every 1.4 days. The object probably migrated into its tight orbit after the star became a white dwarf, surviving the journey intact.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Astronomers have found that red giants swallow every planet that orbits them, no matter how far away it is.
Astronomers have found what is likely a giant planet close to a white dwarf, which suggests such planets can survive there.
Vanderburg and colleagues found that the debris around white dwarfs comes from planets about the size of Jupiter.
Researchers think that WD 1856+534 became a white dwarf much more quickly than most stars do.
items.explanation: The text explains that no intact planet had been found orbiting close to a white dwarf, then reports that Vanderburg and colleagues found an object, very likely a Jupiter-sized planet, in such an orbit, one that probably got there and survived after the star became a white dwarf. Choice B states this finding and what it suggests.

A.why_wrong: The text says red giants engulf planets that orbit close to them, not every planet no matter how far away.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions debris from disintegrated planets around white dwarfs, but it never says that debris comes from Jupiter-sized planets.

D.why_wrong: The text never says how quickly WD 1856+534 became a white dwarf compared with other stars.

sources.what: Vanderburg et al., Nature 2020 (A giant planet candidate transiting a white dwarf), abstract: close-orbiting planets are engulfed in the red giant phase; debris of rocky planets seen around white dwarfs but no intact planets in close orbits; giant planet candidate, roughly Jupiter-sized, transiting WD 1856+534 every 1.4 days; findings indicate giant planets can be scattered into tight orbits without being tidally disrupted

items.notes: Natural science (astronomy). The passage keeps the paper’s candidate status (very likely a planet).

items.passage:
The following text is from Sheila Kaye-Smith’s 1916 novel Sussex Gorse. Reuben’s brother Harry, severely injured and blinded in an accident, is being nursed at home.

Reuben was glad to escape into his farm work. The atmosphere of sickness was like a cloud, which grew blacker and blacker the nearer one came to its heart. Its heart was that little room in the gable, where he spent those wretched nights, disturbed by Harry’s moaning. Out of doors, in the yard or the cowshed or the stable, he breathed a cleaner atmosphere. The heaviness, the vague remorse, grew lighter.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Reuben is frustrated that his farm work keeps him from helping to care for his brother.
Reuben worries that the cold air outdoors will make Harry’s illness worse.
Reuben feels relief when he leaves the gloom of the sickroom to work outdoors.
Reuben sleeps in the stable so that Harry’s moaning will not keep him awake.
items.explanation: The text says Reuben “was glad to escape into his farm work” and describes the sickness in the house as a dark cloud. Outdoors he “breathed a cleaner atmosphere,” and his heaviness “grew lighter.” He feels relief when he gets away from the sickroom to work.

A.why_wrong: Reuben is glad to escape into his farm work; he is not frustrated by it.

B.why_wrong: The text never mentions cold air or any worry that being outdoors could harm Harry.

D.why_wrong: The text says Reuben spends his nights in the little room in the gable, where Harry’s moaning disturbs him.

sources.what: Sheila Kaye-Smith, Sussex Gorse: The Story of a Fight (1916), paragraph copied exactly up to “grew lighter” (Project Gutenberg 56984); Harry was blinded by injuries in an accident earlier in the chapter

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt trimmed at a sentence boundary before the paragraph’s last sentence (about Boarzell), which would need more context. Kaye-Smith is not in any official item or ours (grep).

items.passage:
The following text is from Hans Aanrud’s 1903 novel Lisbeth Longfrock (translated by Laura E. Poulsson in 1907). Lisbeth, a girl from an impoverished family, has come to Hoel, a prosperous neighboring farm, on an errand for her mother.

Lisbeth Longfrock stayed a long time at Hoel that day. Although she had come in the important character of spinning woman, she had never imagined that a great person like Kjersti Hoel would be so pleasant and kind to her. Kjersti treated her to coffee and cakes and milk and other good things, just as if she had been an invited guest, and chatted with her in such a way that Lisbeth forgot all about being shy. And oh, how many curious things Kjersti showed her!
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Lisbeth is surprised and pleased by how warmly Kjersti Hoel receives her.
Lisbeth is too shy to talk with Kjersti Hoel during her long visit to the farm.
Lisbeth hopes that Kjersti Hoel will hire her to work at Hoel when she is older.
Lisbeth is disappointed that Kjersti Hoel treats her as a guest instead of as a worker.
items.explanation: Lisbeth “had never imagined” that a great person like Kjersti Hoel would be so pleasant and kind to her. Kjersti treats her like an invited guest, and Lisbeth forgets her shyness. She is surprised and pleased by her warm welcome.

B.why_wrong: The text says Kjersti chatted with her so that Lisbeth “forgot all about being shy.”

C.why_wrong: The excerpt says nothing about Lisbeth hoping to work at Hoel.

D.why_wrong: Being treated like an invited guest delights Lisbeth; nothing suggests she is disappointed.

sources.what: Hans Aanrud, Lisbeth Longfrock, translated from the Norwegian by Laura E. Poulsson (Boston: Ginn, 1907), paragraph copied exactly (Project Gutenberg 26348); Norwegian original Sidsel Sidsærk, 1903 (Norwegian Wikipedia, Hans Aanrud)

items.notes: Literary prose (translation, like 1.1 Heidi). Aanrud is not in any official item or ours (grep).

items.passage:
The following text is from Władysław Reymont’s 1904 novel The Peasants (translated by Michael H. Dziewicki in 1924). Kuba, a farmhand, has delivered a gift of partridges to the village priest, who has invited him into his residence.

Kuba accordingly entered the passage, but stopped at the threshold of the room. He feared to go in, and would only look through the open door at the various pictures that hung against the walls. He crossed himself, and breathed a devout sigh, so dazzled by the splendour he saw, that the tears started to his eyes, and he felt like saying prayers. Only he was afraid to kneel down upon the polished slippery floor, lest he should soil it.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Kuba most likely feel as he stands at the threshold of the room?
options: He feels impatient because the priest is keeping him waiting in the passage.
He feels disappointed because the room is plainer than he had expected.
He feels curious because he wants to know who painted the pictures on the walls.
He feels awed because the room seems too splendid for someone like him to enter.
items.explanation: Kuba fears to go in, is so “dazzled by the splendour” that tears come to his eyes, and is afraid to kneel on the polished floor “lest he should soil it.” These details show that he is awed by the room and feels unworthy to enter it.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests impatience; Kuba stops at the threshold by his own choice because he fears to go in.

B.why_wrong: Kuba is dazzled by the splendor of the room, so he does not find it plain.

C.why_wrong: Kuba looks at the pictures, but the text gives no sign that he wonders who painted them; his reaction is reverent awe.

sources.what: Władysław Reymont, The Peasants, vol. 1, Autumn (Polish Chłopi, 1904), translated by Michael H. Dziewicki (New York: Knopf, 1924), chapter 4, paragraph copied exactly (Project Gutenberg 75846)

items.notes: Literary prose (translation). Feeling inferred from actions, as in 1.15. Reymont is not in any official item or ours (grep).
